chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
title: Art Tatum as a person: cards, photographic memory and beer
summary: Tatum, about 90 percent blind, remembered every card in pinochle and Collins always partnered with him; they drank heavily together.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Art Tatum: the legend, the piano and the man

blocks.x: We've touched sort of lightly on Art Tatem. I know you were with him on two different occasions. The first time I think was for two years in Chicago. But we haven't really talked at any great length about Tatem. What was he like?

Well, he was very fine person, a great -- as we know he's a great musician, and a great card player. You know, he's had -- I would say he -- he wasn't totally blind, he -- let's say, I would say he was 90 percent blind though. But he could -- he had a photographic memory, and we would play -- when we were at the Three Deuces in Chicago we -- he loved to play cards, and we would play the boss, Sam Beards, and whoever, and Art and I would always team up. And Art would remember every card that hit the board, you know, he would take it up and put it very close to his eyes to see what the number -- you know, what card it was. He remembered what everyone played, and -- in other words we never lost.

We would drink so much we couldn't work sometimes -- I couldn't, he could. But he -- you know, because Art loved to drink, as you know. And drink or smell, that's what we would call him. So they would smell and buy and we would drink.

But he loved to play cards, and when we -- he was a great pinochle player. When we had the trio with Slam Stewart and Art and myself, now this was just before I joined Nat Cole, he and Slam would just play pinochle all night long. He wouldn't let -- Slam was almost a captive. He couldn't get out, you know, he couldn't get away from Art after the job. He just had to play cards.
